query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: The complex phase behavior of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is primarily driven by progressive elemental segregation during cooling that gives rise to local elastic lattice strains. These strains, arising from atomic size mismatches and differential diffusion among Cr, Co, Fe, Ni, and Al, destabilize the high‐temperature BCC state and trigger nucleation of secondary ordered or intermetallic phases (such as σ or B2) upon subsequent thermal exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature, supersaturated BCC solid solution state
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal treatments consisting of varied cooling rates (rapid quench versus slow cooling) followed by isothermal annealing at intermediate to high temperatures (e.g., 600–900 °C)
generation.conditions: The hypothesis should apply when the cooling rate permits sufficient atomic mobility for element partitioning and segregation (i.e., under slower cooling or prolonged annealing conditions) and when the temperature is high enough to mobilize atoms; it may not apply for extremely rapid quenching where segregation is suppressed or at low temperatures with negligible diffusion.
generation.structural_mediator: Local elemental segregation that creates elastic strain fields and lattice distortions within the BCC matrix
generation.mechanism: Due to differences in atomic radii and diffusion rates among the constituent elements, cooling causes nonuniform segregation. This segregation produces elastic lattice stresses that eventually lower the kinetic barrier for transformation, so that upon thermal exposure the strained regions act as nucleation sites for secondary phases (e.g., ordered B2 or σ-phases), thus modifying the overall phase assemblage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline rapid-quench sample that remains predominantly single-phase BCC, samples that cool more slowly or are held at elevated temperatures will exhibit clear signatures of phase decomposition – such as the appearance of new diffraction peaks corresponding to secondary phases, identifiable chemical inhomogeneities (via SEM-EDS or APT), and modifications in mechanical properties (e.g., increased hardness due to stress concentrations and interphase boundaries).
generation.baseline: A rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy that preserves a largely homogeneous, metastable BCC structure with minimal elemental segregation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate when cooling conditions allow atomic mobility and segregation; it may not be significant for conditions (extremely high cooling rates or temperatures too low for diffusion) that prevent sufficient element partitioning. It also assumes the absence of confounding factors such as excessive impurities that might otherwise alter phase stability.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of segregation and the quantitative threshold of lattice strain required for triggering secondary phase nucleation remain unclear. The impact of minor variations in composition or processing impurities on this mechanism is also uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples: one set is rapidly quenched to preserve the BCC state with minimal segregation (baseline) and the other is cooled slowly to allow elemental segregation. Subject both sets to identical annealing treatments (e.g., 600–900 °C for 1 hour). Characterize each sample using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for microstructural and compositional analysis, and microhardness testing for mechanical behavior.
measurements: XRD peak analysis to monitor the emergence of secondary phases
SEM imaging and EDS mapping to assess the extent of elemental segregation
Microhardness measurements to detect changes from elastic stress and phase transformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed, slowly cooled samples do not exhibit any significant differences in phase composition, chemical segregation, or mechanical properties compared to the rapidly quenched samples (i.e., if both sets remain predominantly BCC without secondary phase formation), then the hypothesis that segregation-induced elastic strains govern phase transformation would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A detailed microstructural evaluation was executed on the crystallographic texture as well as the mechanisms for nucleation, phase transformation, and grain growth in a Al0.7CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy. The microstructure and crystallographic orientations were characterized by electron backscatter diffraction, and the chemical composition variations by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. The cast Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy started in the BCC phase and partially transformed into the FCC phase. It was found that the Pitsch orientation relationship (OR) dominates the nucleation mechanism of the FCC phase; however, deviations with respect to the Pitsch OR are observed and are attributed to the differently sized atoms forming an ordered B2 phase in the alloy causing lattice distortions. The dual phase BCC–FCC microstructure contains FCC Widmanstätten plates oriented parallel to the {110}BCC planes of the parent grain. It was found that the crystal orientation distribution after the BCC–FCC phase transformation is confined and is explained as a product of the governing mechanisms.

AbstractIn the present study, powder of FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 HEA was manufactured by gas atomization process, and then used for laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) and microplasma spraying (MPS) technologies. The processes of phase composition and microstructure transformation during above mentioned processes and subsequent heat treatment were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and differential thermal analysis (DTA) methods. It was found that gas atomization leads to a formation of dendrites of body centered cubic (BCC) supersaturated solid solution with insignificant Mo-rich segregations on the peripheries of the dendrites. Annealing leads to an increase of element segregations till to decomposition of the BCC solid solution and formation of σ-phase and B2 phase. Microstructure and phase composition of L-PBF sample are very similar to those of the powder. The MPS coating has a little fraction of face centered cubic (FCC) phase because of Al oxidation during spraying and formation of regions depleted in Al, in which FCC structure becomes more stable.
